question: What happens if a user tries to rename a file to the same name as an existing file in the same folder?

options.text: The file extension is automatically changed.
Windows displays an error: "A file with this name already exists."
Windows appends a number to the new filename (e.g., Document (2).txt).
Windows merges the contents of both files.

solution:
The Correct answer is __**Windows displays an error: "A file with this name already exists."**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• When a user attempts to rename a file to the same name as an **existing file** in the same folder on **Windows**, the operating system checks if there is already a file with that name.
 
• If a file with the same name exists, Windows prevents the renaming action by displaying an **error message**, which reads: "**A file with this name already exists.**"
 
• This mechanism ensures that no two files in the same folder have the **same name**, as it would lead to conflicts in file management.
 
• File names in Windows are used as **unique identifiers** within a folder, and duplication is not allowed.
 
• The error helps maintain the **file system integrity** and avoids overwriting or unintended data loss.
 
• To rename a file successfully, users must ensure that the new file name is **unique** within the folder.
 
• This feature is applicable to all **Windows versions** and is a fundamental rule of file management systems.
